title: A watch study matched office screening. It is not a diagnosis.
friendlyTitle: A watch study can flag high blood pressure. It cannot diagnose it.
summary: Google Research reports a model that uses a consumer watch's pulse and motion sensors, with no cuff calibration, to estimate sustained high blood pressure. In 196 people not on blood-pressure medication, initial screening sensitivity was 65.8% and specificity 90.0% against 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, compared with 55.3% sensitivity for an office cuff reading.
friendlySummary: Google tested whether a normal smartwatch, using its pulse and motion sensors, can spot signs of high blood pressure without a cuff. In a study of 196 people, it found more true cases than a single office reading, and it rarely flagged people who did not have high blood pressure.
whyItMatters: Google says the findings helped inform a Health app trend feature, and later in the same post says the methods are exploratory and not a product diagnosis. A nudge to get checked is the practical use. A watch score is not a cuff result.
friendlyWhyItMatters: This may help someone notice a risk and book a real check. It does not replace a blood-pressure cuff or a doctor's diagnosis.
